Dynamic response paths

Source: R/response.R
psp_response_path.Rd

Traces how a change in a regressor propagates over time in a dynamic model (psp_dynamic()): the shock changes the outcome probabilities in the period it occurs (the short-run impact), which changes the outcomes, which enter the next periods through the lagged outcomes (lag_y, W_lag_y), and so on.

Usage

psp_response_path(
  fit,
  variable,
  shock = 1,
  start = NULL,
  units = NULL,
  type = c("temporary", "permanent"),
  draws = 200,
  nsim = 20,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

fit

A fitted psprobit object.

variable

Name of the regressor to shock.

shock

Size of the change in variable.

start

Period (a value of the time index) in which the shock starts; default the first modelled period.

units

Identifiers of the shocked units (default: all units).

type

"temporary" (the shock lasts one period) or "permanent" (it lasts from start to the last period).

draws

Number of posterior draws.

nsim

Number of simulated outcome histories per draw.

seed

Optional seed for the simulation.

Value

An object of class psp_response: a list with summary, a data frame with the posterior mean, sd and 95% interval of the response by horizon (0 = start period), period, category (ordered models) and units ("all" averages the change over every unit; when only some units are shocked, "shocked" averages over them and "others" over the remaining ones), and draws, the responses for each posterior draw. print() and plot() methods are available.

Details

For each posterior draw, outcome histories are simulated forward from the start period under the baseline (the observed regressors) and under the shock, with the same random numbers in both scenarios. Outcomes before the start period are the observed ones. In every period the outcome probabilities given the simulated history are computed exactly, and the response is their average difference between the two scenarios. The simulation conditions on the posterior draws of the random effects kept by the sampler (as psp_ppc() does), so it describes the sample units. Correlated-random-effects columns (mean_x, cre_x_*) and the initial conditions are held fixed.

With latent dynamics (psp_dynamic(latent = TRUE)) the shock propagates through the latent mean, \(\Delta m_{t+h} = (\gamma S^{-1})^h \Delta m_t\), and the responses are computed exactly from the reduced form (no simulation; nsim is unused). Static models are accepted too; their responses vanish after the shock ends.

Examples

W <- psp_weights(rook_weights(5, 5), style = "W")
d <- sim_psprobit(W, T = 6, beta = c(-0.3, 1, -1), rho = 0.3, gamma = 0.8, seed = 1)
fit <- psprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, d, c("id", "time"), W, dynamic = psp_dynamic(),
                impacts = FALSE,
                control = psp_control(iter = 300, warmup = 200, chains = 1, seed = 1))
#> Warning: Possible convergence problems (R-hat > 1.01 or bulk ESS < 100) for: (Intercept), x1, x2, lag_y, init_y, mean_x1, mean_x2, rho, sigma_alpha. Consider more iterations.
psp_response_path(fit, "x1", draws = 50, nsim = 5, seed = 1)
#> Response of P(y = 1) to a temporary shock of 1 in x1 (50 draws x 5 histories)
#> 
#> Average change over all units:
#>  horizon period   mean     sd   q2.5  q97.5
#>        0      2 0.2352 0.0671 0.1195 0.3668
#>        1      3 0.1078 0.0646 0.0234 0.2410
#>        2      4 0.0498 0.0466 0.0015 0.1614
#>        3      5 0.0254 0.0338 0.0000 0.0925
#>        4      6 0.0149 0.0229 0.0000 0.0755
